summary: This program defines a RobotPet class whose objects store a name, battery level, and mood, and adds a method that decides whether a pet has enough battery for a walk of a given length. Three pets are created and each is asked whether it can manage a 30-minute walk.

lines.text: This begins the blueprint for a robot pet. Everything indented beneath it belongs to the class rather than to any single pet.
The `__init__` method runs automatically whenever a new pet is created, and it receives the starting values for that pet.
Storing the argument on `self` attaches it to this particular pet, so each object remembers its own name.
A method is a function that belongs to the class. Because `duration` is a parameter, the same method can answer the question for a walk of any length.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring documents what the method does in the code itself, which is where a reader will look for it first.
This is the rule the method is built on: every minute of walking costs two units of battery.
The comparison produces True or False, and `return` hands that answer back to whoever called the method.
Calling the class like a function creates one object from the blueprint, passing the three values through to `__init__`.
Dot notation reads the attributes back out of the object, and the f-string drops them straight into the text.
The `\n` escape prints a blank line first, separating the two sections of output.
Here the method is called on a specific pet, so it compares 30 minutes against Rover's own battery. Sparky's 60 is exactly enough, while Beep's 45 is not.
